title: A drink for a thirsty dog
told: a story the Prophet ﷺ told

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever stopped to help an animal? a bird, a stray, a lost pet?
options: then you’ll know this man. listen.
that’s okay. this one might change that.

steps.line: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once told of a man walking a desert road. He grew so thirsty that he climbed down into a well and drank.
When he climbed out, he saw a dog, panting, licking the damp earth because it was so thirsty.

steps.q: The well is deep and he has no bucket. What do you think he does?
o: Walks on; it’s only a dog
Fills his leather sock with water
Waits for someone with a rope
steps.why: His khuff, a leather sock worn over the foot. He climbs out holding it in his teeth, because he needs both hands.

steps.line: “This dog is as thirsty as I was,” he thought. He climbed down again, filled his leather sock, held it in his teeth, and climbed up.

steps.q: “This dog is as thirsty as I was.” Why does that one thought matter?
o: It’s when he sees the dog’s thirst as his own
It’s when he starts hoping for a reward
It’s when he feels guilty for drinking first
steps.why: He had felt that exact thirst minutes before. Mercy often starts with “that was me,” before any thought of reward.

steps.line: He gave the dog water. And God thanked him for it, the Prophet ﷺ said, and forgave him.

steps.q: The companions asked: is there reward even for kindness to animals? What do you think he said?
steps.why: His words were “in every moist liver there is reward”: in anything alive. Even a stray in the desert.

steps.line: “Is there reward for us even with animals?” the companions asked. “In every living thing,” he said, “there is reward.”
Every prayer says it: “Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.” Rabb, Lord, is the one who raises and tends. Worlds, plural: people, animals, everything.

steps.q: The Prophet ﷺ also told of a woman who did wrong to a cat. What had she done?
o: Chased it out of the mosque
Kicked it in front of her neighbors
Shut it in and never fed it
steps.why: She shut the cat in and neither fed it nor let it hunt. Collections like Bukhari’s keep the two stories close together: mercy to an animal counts, and so does cruelty.

steps.line: Today, in a summer heat wave, a shopkeeper sets a bowl of water by her door. For whoever comes: a cat, a dog, a sparrow.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Some old Ottoman mosques have something built into their walls for animals. What?
o: Bells to warn birds off the domes
steps.why: Builders added little bird houses to mosques and bridges, some shaped like tiny mosques. Some cities also kept charitable trusts that fed stray animals.

say: here’s what i love. the man could have walked on. instead he went back down the same well, for a thirsty dog that could never thank him.
in islam, God is rabb al-‘alamin, the one who raises and tends every world. and the prophet ﷺ taught that kindness to any living thing carries reward.

steps.q: God thanked a man for watering a stray dog. What does that suggest “Lord of the worlds” includes?
o: Every creature, even ones nobody notices
steps.why: Just a thirsty dog by a road, and God thanked the man who helped it. It was still inside the worlds God tends.

today.say: today, put out a little water for something that lives near you: a bowl by the door, a dish for the birds, a plant that’s gone dry. a small share in tending the worlds.
options: lovely. that’s exactly what the man did.
beautiful. tending something small is the whole lesson.

card.from: a story the Prophet ﷺ told
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 2363; also 173, 2466 and 6009; Sahih Muslim 2244 (Abu Hurayrah: a man on the road, very thirsty, went down a well and drank; saw a dog panting and eating moist earth from thirst; “this dog has reached the thirst I reached”; filled his khuff (leather sock) with water, held it in his mouth, climbed up and gave the dog water; God thanked him and forgave him; “Is there reward for us in animals?” “In every moist liver there is reward”)
Qur’an 1:2 (“Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds,” Pickthall)
Rabb as the one who raises a thing stage by stage: al-Raghib al-Isfahani, al-Mufradat; al-‘alamin as every kind of created being: Ibn Kathir on 1:2
check: Another version (Bukhari 3467; Muslim 2245) tells of a sinful woman of the Children of Israel who watered a dog; this lesson uses the man’s version (2363). Confirm.
“Rabb, the one who raises and tends” follows al-Raghib’s gloss (bringing a thing to completion stage by stage), not the verse itself. Confirm.
